steps.tx: Pediatric hip pathology divides into two major eponymous entities: **Legg-Calve-Perthes disease** and slipped capital femoral epiphysis. Legg-Calve-Perthes disease involves idiopathic self-limiting avascular necrosis of the proximal femoral epiphysis in children aged four to eight years, predominantly affecting boys. Conversely, slipped capital femoral epiphysis occurs in overweight adolescents aged eleven to fourteen years during the pubertal growth spurt.
steps.say: Perthes disease and slipped capital femoral epiphysis are the two major hip conditions of childhood. Perthes is idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head in active boys aged four to eight. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis is a displacement of the growth plate in overweight adolescents aged eleven to fourteen.

steps.tx: Comparative anteroposterior pelvic films contrast two hip problems. In boys aged four to eight, **Legg-Calve-Perthes disease** is self-limiting bone death in the femoral head from lost blood supply, and the Herring lateral pillar grade records collapse of the outer head. Adolescents from eleven to fourteen years, in the growth spurt, show a Klein line along the superior femoral neck that misses the epiphysis, the Trethowan sign of slipped capital femoral epiphysis.

steps.tx: The radiographic staging of Perthes disease follows Waldenstrom four sequential phases: initial avascular necrosis, fragmentation, reossification, and final healed remodeling. The **Herring lateral pillar** classification on anteroposterior radiographs predicts long-term femoral sphericity based on height preservation of the lateral third of the capital epiphysis: Group A maintains one hundred percent height, Group B retains over fifty percent, and Group C loses over fifty percent, carrying a poor prognosis.
steps.say: Perthes progresses through four Waldenstrom stages: necrosis, fragmentation, reossification, and remodeling. The Herring lateral pillar classification predicts outcome. It measures the height of the outer third of the femoral head: group A has full height, group B retains over half, and group C collapses to under half height, leading to severe deformities.

vis.title: Herring Lateral Pillar Classification
rows: Surgical containment if over 8 years old

steps.tx: The overarching therapeutic objective in Perthes disease is biological **containment of the femoral head**. The softened, revascularizing capital epiphysis is maintained deeply seated within the concentric spherical acetabular cup, which acts as a biological mould preventing lateral extrusion and hinge abduction. Containment is achieved conservatively using an Atlanta abduction orthosis, or surgically via a proximal femoral varus derotation osteotomy or Salter innominate osteotomy.
steps.say: The central rule of Perthes treatment is containment. The softened femoral head must be kept seated deeply inside the round acetabulum so the socket acts as a spherical mould while the bone rebuilds. If the head squirts outward, it deforms permanently. Keep it inside using an abduction brace or femoral varus osteotomy.

right.title: Surgical Options
points: Triple pelvic osteotomy in older children

steps.tx: In slipped capital femoral epiphysis, the femoral neck slips anteriorly and superiorly while the capital epiphysis remains securely within the acetabulum, producing relative **posterior and inferior displacement** of the head. Physical examination demonstrates an obligatory external rotation deformity: as the examiner passively flexes the affected hip, the limb automatically rotates into external rotation due to the posteroinferior physeal shear.
steps.say: In SCFE, the femoral neck slips upward and forward, so the head ends up displaced downward and backward. On examination, look for obligatory external rotation. As you passively flex the child hip up toward ninety degrees, the thigh automatically twists outward into external rotation because of the tilted growth plate.

left.title: Klein Line Alignment
points: Drawn along superior femoral neck on AP view
Fails to intersect epiphysis in SCFE

right.title: Obligatory External Rotation
points: Hip automatically rotates out upon flexion
Loss of internal rotation in flexion

steps.tx: Definitive management of slipped capital femoral epiphysis requires urgent **in situ pinning** using a single central cannulated cancellous screw to arrest further displacement. Attempting forceful closed reduction of a stable slip is strictly contraindicated because manipulation damages tenuous ascending retinacular vessels, causing catastrophic avascular necrosis. Fixation is performed in situ across the center of the physis, achieving physeal fusion.
steps.say: Treat SCFE with emergency single in situ cannulated screw fixation. Never attempt forceful closed reduction of a stable slip. Forcible manipulation tears the posterior retinacular blood vessels and causes avascular necrosis. Simply screw the displaced head right where it sits, which locks the growth plate and stimulates fusion.

quiz.q: What pathognomonic physical sign is elicited during passive hip flexion in an adolescent with slipped capital femoral epiphysis?
options: Obligatory external rotation of the lower limb
Complete absence of femoral head translation
Sudden sharp internal rotation into full abduction
quiz.explain: Obligatory external rotation during passive hip flexion is the hallmark clinical physical finding of SCFE, caused by the posterior-inferior displacement of the femoral head relative to the neck.

quiz.q: Why is forceful closed reduction strictly contraindicated in stable slipped capital femoral epiphysis?
options: It tears the posterior retinacular vessels, provoking avascular necrosis
It causes irreversible tearing of the ligamentum teres
It converts a stable slip into an unstable open pelvic break
It triggers acute reflex sympathetic dystrophy of the knee
quiz.explain: Forceful closed reduction kinks or lacerates the delicate posterior retinacular blood supply of the femoral head, increasing the risk of avascular necrosis from <2% up to 50%.
